text:
Emily: customer reported 429s even though they say they only have ~50 req/s. Attached repro steps from them. They see errors across multiple API keys and projects. Can someone help triage?

Kai: Can you paste the customer's raw response body and the response headers? Most of the time the X-RateLimit headers tell us which scope fired. If they don't have headers that's interesting — might be an edge path in the quota service.

Emily: Paste from customer (redacted API keys):
```
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Content-Type: application/json
Retry-After: 10
{
  "error": {
    "type": "rate_limit_exceeded",
    "message": "Rate limit exceeded"
  }
}
```
Headers they sent back only include Retry-After, no X-RateLimit-Remaining/Limit. They say the failure is happening for API key pk_live_ABC... and also for another key pk_live_XYZ... in a different project.

Nora: I checked Console -> Quotas for that org (org-id O-92f). The org-level token budget is fine. But there's a legacy IP-based policy active for one of their early projects (project-id P-17). That policy has a very small burst window (200 tokens / minute) and that can cause 429s without X-RateLimit-* headers because the IP-shaper sits in front of the quota service and returns the generic 429.

Kai: Good call. Two important notes: (1) our enforcement order is: API-key-specific limits (per-key), then project-level quotas, then org-level budgets. IP-based shapers are enforced in the front-proxy and can short-circuit and return a minimal 429 (sometimes without the extended headers). (2) If multiple scopes are hit we usually attach a header identifying the scope, but front-proxy 429s may not.

Sandeep: I pulled billing/account history for O-92f. They did exceed their committed monthly quota a week ago and we automatically applied a soft-throttle on burst capacity while billing reconciliation happened — this is a protective behavior for some legacy orgs. That could explain why different keys across projects see failures during bursts.

Emily: So we have three possible overlapping causes: per-key limits, legacy IP shaper on P-17, and temporary billing soft-throttle. Customer insists it started after they rotated keys last week. Any auth edge cases to consider?

Kai: One auth edge case: if the customer rotates keys but re-uses the same IP and the front-proxy has a cached token-to-IP mapping, a bug we fixed last quarter could temporarily map the new key to the old project's shaper for ~30–60s. But that was patched — still worth confirming their request timestamps vs rotation time. Ask them for the exact key create timestamps.

Emily: I've asked the customer for the key creation timestamps and a narrow reproduction curl. Meanwhile I ran a local repro using their pattern and hit this curl (useful for others who want to repro):
```
curl -i -X POST "https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat" \\\
  -H "Authorization: Bearer pk_live_ABC..." \\\
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \\\
  -d '{"model":"redwood-1","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"t=short"}] }'
```
Run a tight loop of 250 requests/s for 30s to see if any project-level shaping steps in.

quota-bot: Automated note: quota-service recorded spikes at 2025-11-04T14:02:05Z for org O-92f and IP 52.23.112.18. Project P-17 shows "ip_shaper_active": true.

Nora: I can see the console view for that project: Project quota: 10k req/min, API key pk_live_ABC has a per-key limit of 5k req/min. The IP shaper is configured to allow 200 req/min burst with smoothing. That definitely explains missing headers + sudden 429s for some keys.

Sandeep: Action items from billing side: The customer hit committed quota earlier but didn't set up auto-overage credit. We can temporarily lift the soft-throttle for 2 hours to let them finish the migration, but they need to accept an overage invoice. I'll open the billing exception ticket and loop in the account manager.

Raj: From product perspective we should make these precedence rules more visible in errors. Proposal: when front-proxy rejects due to IP shaper, include an `X-RateLimit-Source: ip-shaper` header and a human-readable hint in the JSON to reduce ambiguous tickets. Filing a small infra/ux task.

Emily: Next steps I told the customer: 1) provide key creation timestamps and the exact IPs/regions for the repro, 2) try repro from a different IP (eg mobile tether) to see if IP shaper is the cause, 3) share a 1-min sample of request IDs for any 429s so we can correlate logs. I'll also ask whether they rotated both keys within 2 mins of each other.

Kai: For internal triage, add these repro steps: collect server logs with these fields: `request_id`, `received_at`, `auth_key_fingerprint`, `project_id`, `org_id`, `src_ip`, `shaper_decision` (if any), `quota_scope` returned. If `shaper_decision` is present that confirms IP-level blocking. Also check `auth_cache` TTL around the rotation time.

Nora: I already toggled the console to show per-IP shaping history and exported the CSV. Sharing it in the ticket.

Sandeep: Billing exception ticket created: BE-3321. Temporary burst lift scheduled for +2h once customer confirms they accept overage.

Emily: Customer replied: they rotated keys at 2025-11-04T13:59:48Z and started seeing 429s at 14:02:03Z. They ran repro from the same CI runner IP. Asking if we can whitelist that CI runner while they sort things.

Kai: Given the timestamps that matches the small window where auth-cache -> proxy mapping could have been stale. We'll look for auth cache hits/misses during 13:59:40–14:02:10. If we confirm cache-mapping issue we should clear that customer's cache entry (we can do a targeted invalidation).

Raj: I'll create a small follow-up to surface `limit-scoping` docs in the console and a tooltip: "Which limit fired?" that links to a KB explaining precedence (API key > Project > Org > IP shaper).

Emily: I'll respond to the customer: offer temporary whitelist (ops-approved, will need their CI runner IP and a signed acceptance of overage terms), tell them to try repro from a new IP, and ask for the 1-min request IDs. Keeping this thread open until we confirm cache mapping and either clear it or lift the throttle.

Kai: If we need a rollback: the patch that fixed mapping last quarter rolled back mapping TTL changes in `auth-cache` and is currently on prod; still, targeted invalidation is safe. If ops wants to do whitelist, escalate to infra-oncall for a short-lived ACL change.

Emily: Closing loop for now — I'll post updates as we get the customer IDs. Thanks all. :thumbsup:
